image.subject: Three colleagues laughing together over lunch at a long wooden table in a sunny Silicon Valley campus courtyard, a manager in a cardigan leaning in to hear a story

storyboard.claim: Casual time together is a deliberate management tactic, not a waste of time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Colleagues laughing over lunch in a sunny courtyard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Picks up the weekend-trip defense with a named concept.
storyboard.addedInformation: The tactic has an academic name: socioemotional communication.

storyboard.claim: The host asks how small talk stops a corporate meltdown.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold question on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Challenges the claim that this is denial.
storyboard.addedInformation: None; the question sets up the mechanism.

image.subject: A tense budget meeting around a long conference table in a glass-walled office, executives leaning forward over printed spreadsheets

storyboard.claim: The hard business debate arrives about ten minutes later.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Tense budget meeting over spreadsheets.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what happens after the small talk.
storyboard.addedInformation: The debate is over budget cuts and resource allocation.

image.subject: A man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer glancing up from a spreadsheet at a colleague, the tension in the room easing

storyboard.claim: When tension spikes, the people already know each other as humans.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two colleagues at a table, the tension softened.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the budget debate from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The humanizing happened earlier, so the disagreement stays professional.

image.subject: Two colleagues in a bright office hallway laughing together, one showing the other a photo of a child in a soccer uniform on a phone

storyboard.claim: Personal talk makes a disagreement less likely to turn personal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Colleagues laughing over a photo of a kid's soccer game.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the example of the connection that came earlier.
storyboard.addedInformation: Examples are a kid's soccer game or a bad flight story.

image.subject: A group of managers around a conference table laughing together, each looking at a colleague with attention and warmth

storyboard.claim: Rapport reminds everyone the others are complex people with lives outside work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A relaxed group of managers around a table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the connection matters.
storyboard.addedInformation: The room sees colleagues as people with families and stress.

image.subject: A wallet-sized family photo propped on a cluttered office desk beside a stack of files and a coffee mug

storyboard.claim: Empathy comes from remembering people have families and stress.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A family photo on an office desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands on the human connection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Empathy is forced into the room by this awareness.

storyboard.claim: The empathy lands before the tension can ignite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold punchline text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the humanization argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: None; a punchline.

image.subject: A manager in a cardigan at an engineering team's desk checking a printed progress chart with a team member, both calm and relaxed

storyboard.claim: Humanizing the boss is maintenance that keeps the team working together.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager reviewing a progress chart with a calm team member.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Agrees with the point that it makes sense.
storyboard.addedInformation: A cohesive team needs people who are not terrified of the boss.

image.subject: A stern executive at the head of a long boardroom table while junior staff sit far down the table, looking anxious and guarded

storyboard.claim: Fear at the head of the table breaks trust across the team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A stern executive at the head of a long table, staff anxious.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the risk when the boss is feared.
storyboard.addedInformation: Colleagues see each other as obstacles to promotion when trust is missing.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, talking with two team members in a relaxed hallway

storyboard.claim: The manager must be humanized in front of the group.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A warm coach talking with team members in a hallway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarizes the group lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: The boss is shown as a human in the public setting.

storyboard.claim: The boardroom is performative, so the ego has to be dismantled there.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold question text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the group setting to the one-on-one.
storyboard.addedInformation: The next question asks what happens behind a closed door.

image.subject: A man in a sport jacket sitting across a small desk from one employee in a closed office, the door shut behind them

storyboard.claim: A one-on-one is a private room with one manager and one employee.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Manager and employee alone at a desk with the door closed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the question about the closed door.
storyboard.addedInformation: Only two people are present, which changes the dynamic.

image.subject: A notepad and pen on a desk in a plain office, a small whiteboard on the wall behind, a chair turned toward an empty seat

storyboard.claim: The one-on-one is where granular coaching happens.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A plain office desk set for a coaching meeting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the one-on-one as the coaching space.
storyboard.addedInformation: Bill had a specific playbook for this setting.

storyboard.claim: The story moves into Bill's actual working environment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Place title on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the general idea to a specific place.
storyboard.addedInformation: The location is the office where Bill ran his one-on-ones.

image.subject: A plain unmarked office door in a Palo Alto office building, with no sign, and a bare desk and whiteboard visible through the glass

storyboard.claim: The office is nondescript, with a desk and a whiteboard and no signage.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An unmarked office door with a bare desk and whiteboard inside.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the place introduced in the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The room has only a desk and a whiteboard.

image.subject: A man in his fifties with short dark hair and a light blazer, engaged and conversational, walks into a plain office holding a notebook, while a stocky white-haired man in his sixties waits behind a desk

storyboard.claim: Jonathan Rosenberg arrives for his scheduled one-on-one with Bill.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg with a notebook entering Bill's office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the people in the scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: The meeting is scheduled and routine.

image.subject: A whiteboard in a plain office with five topics written in a neat numbered list, a marker tray below it

storyboard.claim: Bill normally writes five topics on the whiteboard in advance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard with five neatly written topics.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the expected format of the meeting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Normally the manager sets the agenda.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties sitting with his hand resting over part of a whiteboard, while a man in a light blazer sits opposite

storyboard.claim: This time Bill does not show Jonathan the topics.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill's hand covering part of the whiteboard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Breaks the expected routine from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Bill withholds his list.

image.subject: A whiteboard whose top half is covered by a cloth, with a clean blank section left visible below it

storyboard.claim: Bill covers the list or points to a blank section of the board.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A whiteboard partly covered by a cloth.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows what the previous beat describes.
storyboard.addedInformation: The blank section is where Jonathan must write.

image.subject: A man in a light blazer writing a list of five items on a whiteboard while a stocky white-haired man in a sport jacket watches from a chair

storyboard.claim: Jonathan must put his top five items on the board first.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Rosenberg writing five items while Bill watches.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what Bill forces Jonathan to do.
storyboard.addedInformation: The manager's list comes after the employee's.

image.subject: An office wall clock showing an early hour above an empty desk with a notepad, a bright Monday morning light through the window

storyboard.claim: Any manager can apply this technique on Monday morning.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A wall clock over an empty desk on a Monday morning.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the master class into an action.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mistake is using one-on-ones for top-down updates.

image.subject: A manager in a cardigan reads a long printed list of demands aloud across a desk while a team member sits with arms crossed

storyboard.claim: Most managers use one-on-ones to read off demands.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager reading a list of demands across a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mistake from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: A one-on-one is not a status report for the manager.

image.subject: A laptop screen showing an email inbox on a desk in an empty office, a coffee mug beside the keyboard

storyboard.claim: A status report belongs in an email, not a one-on-one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An email inbox on a laptop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the alternative to the status report.
storyboard.addedInformation: The one-on-one shows how the employee prioritizes time and energy.

image.subject: A magnifying glass lying on a printed page of handwritten to-do notes on a wooden desk

storyboard.claim: The one-on-one is a diagnostic tool.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A magnifying glass over handwritten notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the one-on-one is useful.
storyboard.addedInformation: Putting their list on the board reveals how the employee thinks.

storyboard.claim: Merging the two lists exposes the gap in thinking.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Three-item list on a plain background.
storyboard.onScreenText: MY LIST, THEIR LIST, THE GAP
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the merge that follows the board exercise.
storyboard.addedInformation: The gap is between what the employee thinks matters and what the manager knows matters.

image.subject: A large strategy map pinned on an office wall with colored zones and arrows, seen from a desk in front of it

storyboard.claim: The manager's broader strategic view shows what truly matters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A strategy map pinned on an office wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the manager's side of the gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: The map contrasts with minor operational concerns.

left.label: EMPLOYEE'S LIST
left.subject: A small handwritten note reading cafeteria food and a tiny bug fix

right.label: MANAGER'S LIST
right.subject: A bold printed chart of a competitor's market share with a red arrow pointing up

storyboard.claim: An employee's minor item is contrasted with a manager's major strategic pivot.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Small handwritten note on one side, competitor chart on the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives a concrete example of the gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: The employee has not considered the competitor at all.

storyboard.claim: The manager has found a blind spot in the employee's prioritization.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold punchline text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the example.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagnosis gives the coach something to act on.

storyboard.claim: Bill's one-on-one framework goes well beyond a list of ongoing work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the diagnosis to the framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sources detail the framework.

storyboard.claim: The host asks what else was on Bill's list.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold question on a plain background.
storyboard.onScreenText: WHAT ELSE WAS ON HIS LIST?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the framework statement.
storyboard.addedInformation: None; the question leads to the answer.

storyboard.claim: The first part of the framework covers job performance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two-item checklist on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question about the list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Performance on job requirements is the first item.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, leaning across a desk and asking a question while an employee listens

storyboard.claim: Bill constantly asks whether the employee gets along with peers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill leaning across a desk asking a question.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the peer-focused part of the framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: He asks about the engineering lead and the marketing director.

image.subject: A manager in a dark blazer sitting at a desk with a colleague, the two talking earnestly about coaching their own team members

storyboard.claim: Bill also asks how employees coach their own direct reports.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two managers talking at a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the framework's management part.
storyboard.addedInformation: Management and leadership is the second theme.

image.subject: A lightbulb sketched on a whiteboard beside a simple process flowchart with arrows looping back

storyboard.claim: Innovation means constantly evaluating systems to get better.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Lightbulb sketch beside a process flowchart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the third theme of the framework.
storyboard.addedInformation: The focus on peer relationships separates Bill's playbook.

image.subject: A tall wooden ladder leaning against a glass office wall in an empty corridor

storyboard.claim: Most corporate structures assume the key relationship is vertical, like a ladder.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A ladder against a glass office wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the contrast with peer relationships.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ladder is the usual assumption about relationships.

storyboard.claim: Bill believed horizontal peer bonds matter more than vertical ones.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bold question on a plain background.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the answer about cross-functional work.
storyboard.addedInformation: None; the question leads to the answer.

image.subject: Two colleagues from different departments shaking hands in a bright open-plan office hallway

storyboard.claim: Real cross-functional work happens between peers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two colleagues shaking hands in a hallway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question about why peers matter.
storyboard.addedInformation: A good coach probes to keep those lateral bonds strong.

left.label: MARKETING VP
left.subject: A man in a sport jacket turning away from a colleague in a cold office

right.label: PRODUCT VP
right.subject: An engineer with a laptop looking away from the manager across a desk

storyboard.claim: If two VPs dislike each other, the company eventually fails.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two executives turned away from each other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the consequence of weak peer bonds.
storyboard.addedInformation: Liking the CEO does not compensate for the rift.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan sitting back in her chair at a desk, waiting while a team member sits across from her

storyboard.claim: A new manager who only waits for the employee looks passive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager sitting back in her chair, waiting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns to the new manager's worry.
storyboard.addedInformation: The manager fears looking like they lack direction.
